original_clauses.source_paraphrase: Reid's complaint alleged that the detective relied solely on a facial-recognition match to seek an arrest warrant.
original_clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A biometric similarity result remains evidence for an investigative lead; it does not independently establish identity, probable cause or authority for detention.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: A facial-recognition similarity result that could validly serve as an investigative lead was promoted into the operative identity basis for warrants and detention without an independent identity basis being adequately established.

original_clauses.source_paraphrase: The complaint said a basic search would have shown Reid was in Georgia when the Louisiana theft occurred, and a reported sheriff's-office email reiterated that facial-recognition results require additional evidence or leads for an arrest warrant.
original_clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: When a consequential workflow requires corroboration, readily available checks capable of falsifying the candidate identity must be completed before the result is represented as warrant-ready.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: The reported workflow omitted basic location and other corroborating checks that were required before a facial-recognition lead could be treated as warrant-ready identity evidence.

original_clauses.source_paraphrase: The warrant affidavit referred to a credible source and still photographs but did not disclose the use of facial-recognition technology, according to Reid's complaint and counsel.
original_clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A consequential reviewer must know when an asserted identity originated as a machine-generated similarity lead so that the inference's uncertainty and corroboration requirements remain visible.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: Omitting the inferential origin made the candidate identity appear more authoritatively grounded within the warrant pathway than the facial-recognition lead alone could support.

baseline_sources.deployment_context: Occurrence-specific reporting based on an interview with Reid, the arrest-warrant account, his federal civil complaint, and responses or non-responses from the detective and sheriff's office.
baseline_sources.evidence_status_basis: Associated Press independently interviewed Reid and reported the arrest, six-day detention and warrant withdrawal while clearly attributing disputed investigative details to his federal complaint; the defendants did not provide a substantive response reported in the article.
baseline_sources.interpretive_reliance: Relied on for the arrest, detention duration, warrant withdrawal, Reid's continuing psychological response, missed work and towing consequence, and the complaint's attributed allegations that the detective relied solely on the facial-recognition match, omitted basic location checks and described the identification source opaquely in the warrant affidavit.
baseline_sources.model_or_algorithm: not fully established in the source

primary_artefact_access.access_method: Direct review of the public Associated Press article.
limitations: The sole-reliance, omitted-investigation and affidavit-description propositions are attributed to Reid's complaint and counsel rather than adjudicated findings.
The article does not identify the facial-recognition vendor, match score, model version or complete investigative record.
The detective declined comment and the sheriff's office declined to comment on pending litigation.

baseline_sources.relevance_note: Preferred occurrence source for the inference-to-arrest pathway, omitted corroboration, six-day liberty deprivation, corrective warrant withdrawal and materialised psychological and economic consequences.
baseline_sources.source_context: AP reports that Reid was arrested in Georgia on Louisiana warrants after facial-recognition technology linked him to a theft, spent six days in jail, and was released after his family retained Louisiana counsel and supplied photographs and video showing material physical differences. The article attributes to Reid's complaint allegations that the detective relied solely on the match, did not perform a basic location check, and described the identification in the warrant affidavit as coming from a credible source without disclosing facial recognition. It also reports a sheriff's-office email stating that facial-recognition matches require additional evidence or leads for an arrest warrant.
baseline_sources.source_title: Facial recognition technology jailed a man for days. His lawsuit joins others from Black plaintiffs
baseline_sources.source_url_status: public source page available at review

baseline_sources.deployment_context: Later reporting on the federal civil-rights litigation, the identification of Clearview AI as the facial-recognition provider, and the May 2025 settlement.
baseline_sources.evidence_status_basis: The report identifies the transferred federal case and reports a finalized $200,000 settlement while expressly noting that the sheriff's office did not admit fault; it is used for later procedural context rather than as an adjudication of liability.
baseline_sources.interpretive_reliance: Relied on to identify Clearview AI as the tool reported in the investigation and to record the May 2025 settlement, Reid's response, the absence of an admission of fault, and the reported post-incident reminder that facial recognition was intended only as a lead requiring additional investigative evidence.
baseline_sources.model_or_algorithm: Clearview AI facial-recognition platform; model version not published

primary_artefact_access.access_method: Direct review of the public Biometric Update report.
limitations: The settlement agreement, payment record and complete federal docket were not directly reviewed.

baseline_sources.source_context: Biometric Update reports that Reid accepted a $200,000 settlement from the Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office on 13 May 2025, without an admission of fault. It identifies Clearview AI as the facial-recognition provider and reports that a January 2023 internal memo reiterated that a facial-recognition result was a lead rather than a basis for arrest and required additional investigative evidence.

baseline_sources.source_url_status: public source page available at review

new_episodes.source_paraphrase: Later reporting says the first identification was reused by a Baton Rouge detective to obtain a second warrant. This is warrant propagation, not a second independent biometric confirmation.
new_episodes.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Repeated use does not add independent assurance to the originating identity inference.

new_episodes.source_paraphrase: Reid was arrested in Georgia and detained for six days. His family obtained Louisiana counsel, who supplied photographs and video showing physical differences; the sheriff’s office requested withdrawal and Reid was released.
new_episodes.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Correction and release must be represented separately from the initial warrant and the harm already materialised.

new_episodes.source_paraphrase: Reporting describes a January 2023 sheriff’s-office message reiterating that facial-recognition results require further evidence for a warrant. This came after the November 2022 arrest.
new_episodes.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Later corrective instructions cannot prove a control was effective before the harm.

new_episodes.source_paraphrase: Reid brought a federal civil case in September 2023 and later accepted a $200,000 settlement in May 2025 without an admission of fault.
new_episodes.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A settlement is a distinct remedial outcome, not a merits finding or the magnitude of the original harm.
